question.text: For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \Bigg( -P \dfrac{\partial g}{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\phantom{A}}} + R \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \] From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \] Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z=g(x,y),$ it can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(x,y) = \left\langle x,\: y,\: g(x,y) \right\rangle. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x & = \left\langle 1, \: 0, \: \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_y & = \left\langle 0, \: 1, \: \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_y &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} \\ 0 & 1 & \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} \end{vmatrix} = \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}, \: -\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}, \: 1 \right \rangle. \end{align*}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(x,y)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_x \times \mathbf{r}'_y) \,\textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \langle P, \: Q, \: R \rangle \cdot \left \langle -\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x}, \: -\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y}, \: 1 \right \rangle \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \Bigg( -P \dfrac{\partial g}{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}{\partial x}} } -Q \dfrac{\partial g}{\bbox[3pt, border:1pt solid black]{\color{blue}{\partial y}} } + R \Bigg) \: \textrm{d}A. \end{align*}

example.title: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral Using a Formula

question.text: Consider the vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z)=\left\langle 2x-z, \: y-z, \: z+y\right\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=4x-y$ for $0 \leq x \leq 2$ and $-1 \leq y \leq 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ can be expressed as \[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \int_{0}^{2} \int_{-1}^{2} \fbox{$\phantom{AAAAAAA}$} \: \text{d}v \: \text{d}u. \] What is the missing expression?
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ for $(u,v) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \,\textrm{d}A. \]

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

\[ \mathbf{r}(u,v) = \left\langle u,\: v,\: 4u-v \right\rangle \]

over the domain

\[ D = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: 0 \leq u \leq 2, \: -1 \leq v \leq 2 \big\}. \]

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_u & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial u} \right\rangle \\[5pt] & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(u), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(v), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial u}(4u-v) \right\rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle 1, \: 0, \: 4 \right\rangle \\[10pt] \mathbf{r}'_v & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v}, \: \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v}, \: \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial v} \right\rangle \\[5pt] & = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(u), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(v), \: \dfrac{\partial}{\partial v}(4u-v) \right\rangle \\[5pt] & = \left\langle 0, \: 1, \: -1 \right\rangle \end{align*}

Now, the fundamental vector product is

\begin{align*} \mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v &= \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ 1 & 0 &4 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \left \langle \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix}, \: -\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 \end{vmatrix}, \: \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \right\rangle \\[5pt] & = \left \langle -4, \: 1, \: 1 \right \rangle. \end{align*}

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $\mathbf{r}(u,v)$ into $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align*} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) &= \left\langle 2x-z, \: y-z, \: z+y \right\rangle \Big|_{x=u,\, \\ y=v,\, \\ z=4u-v} \\[5pt] &= \left\langle 2u-(4u-v), \: v-(4u-v), \: 4u-v+v \right\rangle \\[5pt] &= \left\langle -2u+v, \: -4u+2v, \: 4u \right\rangle \end{align*}

Then, we calculate the dot product of $\mathbf{F}$ and $\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v{:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) &= \left\langle-2u+v, \: -4u+2v, \: 4u \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle -4, \: 1, \: 1 \right\rangle \\[3pt] &=(-2u+v) \cdot (-4) + (-4u+2v) \cdot 1 + 4u \cdot 1 \\[3pt] &= 8u - 4v + -4u+2v + 4u \\[3pt] &= 8u-2v. \end{align}

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \left\langle 2x-z, \: y-z, \: z+y \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(u,v)) \cdot (\mathbf{r}'_u \times \mathbf{r}'_v) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D ( 8u-2v) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2} \int_{-1}^{2} {\color{blue} (8u-2v)} \: \textrm{d}v \: \textrm{d}u. \end{align*}

question.text:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

\[ \mathbf F(x, y, z) = \left\langle \cos^2(xy), \: \cos^2(xy), \: 1 \right\rangle, \]

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\tan(xy)$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $-x \leq y \leq 0.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(\tan(xy)) = \dfrac{y}{\cos^2(xy)} \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(\tan(xy)) = \dfrac{x}{\cos^2(xy)} \end{align*}

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \left\langle \cos^2(xy), \: \cos^2(xy), \: 1 \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \]

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) &= \left\langle \cos^2(xy), \: \cos^2(xy), \: 1\right\rangle \Big|_{z=\tan(xy)} \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{\cos^2(xy)}_{P}, \: \underbrace{\cos^2(xy)}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{1}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \left\langle \cos^2(xy), \: \cos^2(xy), \: 1 \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \left( -(\cos^2(xy)) \cdot \left(\dfrac{y}{\cos^2(xy)}\right) - (\cos^2(xy)) \cdot \left(\dfrac{x}{\cos^2(xy)}\right) + 1 \right) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -y - x + 1\big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \int_{-x}^0 \big( -y - x + 1\big) \: \mathrm d y \: \mathrm d x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left[ -\dfrac{y^2}{2} - xy + y \right]_{y=-x}^{y=0} \: \mathrm d x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left(\dfrac{x^2}{2} - x^2 + x\right) \: \mathrm d x \\[5pt] &= \int_0^1 \left(-\dfrac{x^2}{2} + x \right) \: \mathrm d x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{x^3}{6} + \dfrac{x^2}{2} \right]_0^1 \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac 16 + \dfrac 12 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 13 \end{align*}

question.text:
Calculate the flux of the vector field

\[ \mathbf F(x, y, z) = \left\langle x+y, \: y-x, \: z \right\rangle, \]

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=1+x^2+y^2$ for $-1 \leq x \leq 1$ and $-1 \leq y \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ given by $z = g(x,y)$ for $(x,y) \in D,$ the flux of a vector field $\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle P,\: Q,\: R \right\rangle$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} = \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A. \]

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y){:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(1+x^2+y^2) = 2x \\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(1+x^2+y^2) = 2y \end{align*}

In this case, the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ is given by \[ \iint\limits_S \left\langle x+y, \: y-x, \: z \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} \]

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $\mathbf F(x,y,z){:}$

\begin{align} \mathbf{F}(x,y,g(x,y)) &= \left\langle x+y, \: y-x, \: z\right\rangle \Big|_{z=1+x^2+y^2} \\[3pt] &= \big\langle \underbrace{x+y}_{P}, \: \underbrace{y-x}_{Q}, \: \underbrace{1+x^2+y^2}_R \big\rangle \end{align}

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S \left\langle x+y, \: y-x, \: z \right\rangle \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S} &= \iint\limits_D \left( -P\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial x} - Q\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial y} + R \right) \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -(x+y) \cdot (2x) - (y-x) \cdot (2y) + 1+x^2+y^2 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \big( -2x^2 -2xy - 2y^2 + 2xy+1+x^2+y^2 \big) \: \textrm{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-1}^{1} \big( 1 - x^2 - y^2 \big) \: \textrm{d}y \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \left[ y - x^2y - \dfrac{y^3}{3} \right]_{y=-1}^{y=1} \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \left[ \left( 1 - x^2 - \dfrac 13 \right) - \left( -1 + x^2 + \dfrac 13\right)\right] \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} \left( 2 - 2x^2 - \dfrac 23 \right) \: \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ 2x - \dfrac{2x^3}{3} - \dfrac 23 x \right]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left( 2 - \dfrac 23 - \dfrac 23\right) - \left( -2 + \dfrac 23 + \dfrac 23 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 43 \end{align*}
